hint: Capitalized Cost (CC) = First Cost + P(A/i) + P(A/F, i, n). Convert all recurring costs to their Present Worth over an infinite life.
shortcut: Capitalized cost just means 'Present Worth of a project that lasts forever'. Use CC = P + (A/i).
fifthGrader: If you wanted to put enough money in a magic bank account today so the interest pays for this pump station forever and ever, how much money do you need? That's Capitalized Cost!

title: Driveway Grading & FFE
description: Determine the required Finished Floor Elevation (FFE) of the main house and garage, distance from the road, and road centerline elevation to ensure positive drainage (rain will not enter the garage). The garage slab is exactly 0.55 ft below the FFE of the house.
hint: Sketch a profile view. Start at the road centerline, subtract the cross slope to the curb, add the curb height, and then calculate the rise along the driveway using its slope and length.
shortcut: Elevation = Starting Elevation + (Slope * Distance). Make sure your slopes are converted from percentages to decimals (e.g., 2% = 0.02).
fifthGrader: Think of this like building a ramp for your toy cars. If the road is the bottom of the ramp, we need to make sure the driveway goes UP to the garage so that water rolls down to the street, not into the house!

title: Driveway Runoff Energy
description: Using the Energy Equation, determine how far horizontally stormwater runoff from the road will travel up a driveway. Evaluate whether the initial kinetic energy of the water will overcome the driveway slope and cause the runoff to enter the garage.
hint: Use Conservation of Energy: Kinetic Energy (Velocity Head) converts to Potential Energy (Elevation Head). V^2 / 2g = Elevation change.
shortcut: Max Distance = (V^2 / 2g) / Driveway Slope.
fifthGrader: Think of rolling a ball up a hill. If you roll it really fast (high velocity), it rolls further up the hill before stopping and rolling back down. If the hill is steep, it stops sooner!

title: CPM Arrow Way: Addition
description:
Using the Arrow Way, what is 245 + 132?

Start at 245 -> +100 -> 345 -> +30 -> 375 -> +2 -> 377
hint: Break 132 into its place values: 100, 30, and 2.
shortcut: Add the hundreds first, then tens, then ones.
fifthGrader: Start at 245. Make a big jump of 100 to 345. Make a medium jump of 30 to 375. Make a tiny hop of 2 to get 377!

title: CPM Arrow Way: Subtraction
description:
Using the Arrow Way, what is 560 - 245?

Start at 560 -> -200 -> 360 -> -40 -> 320 -> -5 -> 315
hint: Break the number you are subtracting (245) into easy backward jumps.
shortcut: Subtract hundreds, then tens, then ones.
fifthGrader: Start at 560. Jump backward 200 to 360. Jump backward 40 to 320. Hop backward 5 to get 315!

title: CPM Arrow Way: Make a 10
description:
Using the Arrow Way, what is 398 + 45?

Start at 398 -> +2 -> 400 -> +43 -> 443
hint: Use 'friendly numbers'. Add 2 to 398 to get 400, then add the rest.
shortcut: Round 398 to 400, add 45 (445), and then subtract the 2 you added (443).
fifthGrader: 398 is so close to 400! Add just 2 to reach 400. Since we took 2 out of the 45, we only have 43 left to add. 400 + 43 = 443!

title: Total Hardness Calculation
description: A water sample contains 60 mg/L of Ca2+ and 24 mg/L of Mg2+. The equivalent weights are Ca2+ = 20.0 mg/meq, Mg2+ = 12.2 mg/meq, and CaCO3 = 50.0 mg/meq. The Total Hardness (TH) in mg/L as CaCO3 is most nearly:
hint: Convert mg/L to mg/L as CaCO3 by multiplying by (50 / Equivalent Weight). TH = Ca Hardness + Mg Hardness.
shortcut: Ca Hardness is approx (mg/L Ca * 2.5). Mg Hardness is approx (mg/L Mg * 4.12). 60 * 2.5 + 24 * 4.12 = 150 + 98.8 = 248.8.
fifthGrader: Think of hardness as the amount of tiny rocks dissolved in the water. We are just putting all the different rocks on the same scale so we can add them up!

title: Carbonate vs Noncarbonate Hardness
description: A water analysis shows Total Hardness = 250 mg/L as CaCO3 and Alkalinity = 180 mg/L as CaCO3. The Carbonate Hardness (CH) and Noncarbonate Hardness (NCH) in mg/L as CaCO3 are respectively most nearly:
hint: If Alkalinity < Total Hardness, then Carbonate Hardness = Alkalinity. Noncarbonate Hardness = Total Hardness - Carbonate Hardness.
shortcut: Just look at the graph! The alkalinity (green) matches up with the hardness. Any hardness hanging over the edge of the green bar is Noncarbonate (purple).
fifthGrader: Carbonate hardness is the part of the hardness that matches the alkalinity. Anything leftover is called noncarbonate!

title: Lime Dosage for Carbonate Hardness
description: A water has a CO2 concentration of 15 mg/L as CaCO3, Ca2+ of 140 mg/L as CaCO3, Mg2+ of 60 mg/L as CaCO3, and Alkalinity of 150 mg/L as CaCO3. What is the stoichiometric lime (CaO) dose required in mg/L as CaCO3 to remove the carbonate hardness?
hint: Lime dose = CO2 + HCO3(Alkalinity) + Mg (if removing Mg). If only removing Ca Carbonate hardness, Lime = CO2 + Alkalinity associated with Ca.
shortcut: For every molecule of bicarbonate alkalinity, you need one molecule of lime. Don't forget to add lime to destroy the free CO2 first!
fifthGrader: Lime is like a chemical sponge. We need enough sponge to soak up the CO2 gas first, and then enough to soak up the carbonate hardness.

title: Soda Ash Dosage
description: A water has Total Hardness = 300 mg/L as CaCO3 and Alkalinity = 200 mg/L as CaCO3. If all Noncarbonate Hardness (NCH) is associated with Calcium, the required Soda Ash (Na2CO3) dose in mg/L as CaCO3 to completely soften the NCH is most nearly:
hint: Soda Ash is used ONLY to remove Noncarbonate Hardness (NCH). Calculate NCH = Total Hardness - Alkalinity.
shortcut: The Soda Ash dose in mg/L as CaCO3 is exactly equal to the Noncarbonate Hardness (NCH). 300 - 200 = 100 mg/L as CaCO3.
fifthGrader: Soda ash is a special powder that only attacks 'Noncarbonate' rocks. We just measure how much noncarbonate rock is in the water and add that exact amount of powder!

title: Excess Lime Softening (Magnesium Removal)
description: To precipitate Magnesium during softening, the pH must be raised to around 11.0. This requires an 'excess lime' dose. If the total Mg2+ is 80 mg/L as CaCO3, and the standard excess lime dose is 35 mg/L as CaCO3, the total lime required for Mg removal (excluding CO2 and HCO3) is:
hint: Lime required for Mg removal = Mg2+ concentration + Excess Lime.
shortcut: Magnesium is stubborn! It requires 1 part lime to react with the alkalinity, 1 part lime to precipitate the Mg, PLUS an extra 35 mg/L to drive the pH to 11.
fifthGrader: Magnesium rocks only melt when the water is super basic (pH 11). We have to add extra 'excess' lime just to push the pH up high enough!

title: Ion Exchange Softening Capacity
description: An ion exchange softener has a resin capacity of 20 kilograins per cubic foot (kgr/ft3). The resin volume is 50 ft3. The raw water has a hardness of 300 mg/L as CaCO3. What is the maximum volume of water (gallons) that can be softened before regeneration?
hint: 1 grain per gallon (gpg) = 17.1 mg/L. Total Capacity (grains) = Volume * Capacity. Gallons = Total Capacity / Hardness (in gpg).
shortcut: Convert 300 mg/L to grains per gallon: 300 / 17.1 = 17.5 gpg. Total grains = 20,000 * 50 = 1,000,000. 1,000,000 / 17.5 = 57,142 gallons.
fifthGrader: Think of the resin like a sponge that can hold exactly 1,000,000 pieces of dirt. If every gallon of water has 17.5 pieces of dirt, how many gallons until the sponge is full?

title: Softened Water Blending (Bypass)
description: A treatment plant must deliver water with a hardness of 100 mg/L. The raw water has a hardness of 350 mg/L, and the ion exchange softener reduces hardness to 10 mg/L. What percentage of the flow should bypass the softener?
hint: Use the mass balance equation: Q_total * C_target = Q_bypass * C_raw + Q_soft * C_soft. Let Q_total = 1.
shortcut: Bypass Fraction = (Target - Softened) / (Raw - Softened). (100 - 10) / (350 - 10) = 90 / 340 = 26.5%.
fifthGrader: If you mix super salty water with pure water, you get medium salty water. We are just using math to figure out the perfect recipe for the mix!

title: Equivalent Weight Conversion
description: A water sample has 96 mg/L of Sulfate (SO4 2-). The atomic weights are S=32.1, O=16.0. The equivalent weight of CaCO3 is 50.0 g/eq. What is the Sulfate concentration in mg/L as CaCO3?
hint: Molecular weight of SO4 = 32.1 + 4(16) = 96.1 g/mol. Charge is 2, so Equivalent Weight = 96.1 / 2 = 48.05 g/eq. Multiply mg/L by (50 / 48.05).
shortcut: The equivalent weight of Sulfate is roughly 48. Since 96 / 48 = 2 meq/L. Multiply by 50 to get 100 mg/L as CaCO3.
fifthGrader: Scientists like to measure everything using the exact same ruler (CaCO3). We are just converting Sulfate's weight into the universal ruler's weight!

title: Alkalinity Relationships
description: A water sample has a pH of 10.2. The Phenolphthalein alkalinity (P) is 40 mg/L as CaCO3 and the Total alkalinity (T) is 120 mg/L as CaCO3. The concentration of Carbonate (CO3 2-) alkalinity is most nearly:
hint: Check the Alkalinity Relationship Table. If P < 1/2 T, then Carbonate = 2*P and Bicarbonate = T - 2P.
shortcut: P = 40, T = 120. Since 40 is less than half of 120, Carbonate is 2 * P = 80 mg/L as CaCO3.
fifthGrader: Alkalinity comes in three flavors: Hydroxide, Carbonate, and Bicarbonate. Depending on the pH, we can figure out exactly how much of each flavor is in the water!

title: Split Treatment Softening
description: In a split treatment softening process, a portion of the raw water bypasses the first stage (excess lime) and is mixed with the first stage effluent in the second stage. The primary purpose of this bypassed flow is to:
hint: The first stage operates at pH 11 to drop out Mg. The bypassed raw water contains HCO3- and CO2, which naturally lowers the pH and provides carbonate to react with excess Ca.
shortcut: Bypassing raw water saves money! You don't need as much CO2 for recarbonation because the raw water naturally neutralizes the high pH of the first stage.
fifthGrader: Instead of adding expensive acid to fix the super basic water from the first tank, we just mix in some normal raw water. It naturally cools off the chemicals and saves money!

title: Gravity Retaining Wall Overturning Stability
description:
A concrete gravity retaining wall having a unit weight of 150 pcf is shown in the figure. The wall is 8 ft high, with a top width of 2 ft and a base width of 4 ft.

The retained granular backfill has a friction angle φ = 32°, cohesion c = 0, and total unit weight γt = 110 pcf. Use Rankine active earth pressure theory and neglect wall friction.

The factor of safety against overturning about the toe at Point O is most nearly:
hint:
1. Calculate Rankine active earth pressure coefficient Ka:
Ka = tan²(45° - φ/2) = (1 - sin 32°) / (1 + sin 32°) = 0.3073

2. Compute total active lateral thrust Pa and overturning lever arm:
Pa = 0.5 × Ka × γ × H² = 0.5 × 0.3073 × 110 × 64 = 1,081.5 lb/ft
Lever arm y = H / 3 = 8 / 3 = 2.667 ft above the base

3. Compute overturning moment MOT about toe Point O:
MOT = Pa × (H/3) = 1,081.5 × 2.667 = 2,884.1 ft-lb/ft

4. Divide the wall into front triangular toe wedge (b=2', h=8') and back rectangular stem (b=2', h=8'). Sum resisting moments about toe Point O:
• W1 = 0.5 × 2 × 8 × 150 = 1,200 lb, arm = ⅔ × 2 = 1.333 ft → MR1 = 1,600 ft-lb
• W2 = 2 × 8 × 150 = 2,400 lb, arm = 2 + 1 = 3.0 ft → MR2 = 7,200 ft-lb
• ΣMR = 1,600 + 7,200 = 8,800 ft-lb/ft

5. Factor of Safety against Overturning (FS_OT):
FS = ΣMR / MOT = 8,800 / 2,884.1 = 3.05 (Rounds to 3.1)
shortcut:
For a trapezoidal gravity wall with a vertical back face, divide into triangle (toe) + rectangle (stem).

• Toe Triangle Centroid: From the sharp toe Point O, the arm is at ⅔ × base = 1.333 ft (NOT ⅓!).
• Stem Rectangle Centroid: From Point O, arm = b_toe + ½ × b_stem = 2 + 1 = 3.0 ft.

⚠️ Classic Distractor Trap: If you accidentally take the triangle centroid at ⅓, your calculated FS will be ~2.7 (Option B)!
fifthGrader:
Think of a heavy book standing upright on a table. If someone pushes sideways against it, the book wants to tip over around its bottom front edge.

To keep it standing, the heavy downward weight of the concrete wall acts like a massive anchor.

We simply compare the overturning torque from the dirt against the resisting torque of the concrete: if the resisting torque is at least 1.5× to 2.0× larger (here it is 3.1× larger), the wall is completely safe from overturning!

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect: Make sure you compute the active lateral thrust Pa = 0.5 * Ka * γ * H² acting at H/3 = 2.67 ft.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect: 2.7 is the classic NCEES distractor trap! The centroid of the triangular toe is 2/3 * b_tri = 1.333 ft from Point O, not 1/3.

options.label: C
options.feedback: ✓ Correct! ΣMR = 8,800 ft-lb/ft, MOT = 2,884.1 ft-lb/ft, yielding FS_OT = 8,800 / 2,884.1 = 3.05 ≈ 3.1.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect: Be sure to divide the wall into triangular and rectangular components rather than assuming a single rectangular block.

title: Retaining Wall Stability with Submerged Backfill & Pore Water Pressure
description:
A concrete gravity retaining wall having a unit weight of 150 pcf is shown in the figure. The wall is 8 ft high, with a top width of 2 ft and a base width of 4 ft.

The retained granular backfill has a friction angle φ = 32°, cohesion c = 0, moist unit weight γ = 110 pcf, and saturated unit weight γsat = 125 pcf.

Due to clogged weep holes after heavy rainfall, the lower 4 ft of the backfill is submerged under a water table (submerged portion hw = 4 ft, unit weight of water γw = 62.4 pcf). Use Rankine active earth pressure theory, neglect wall friction, and neglect base uplift.

The factor of safety against overturning about the toe at Point O is most nearly:
hint:
1. Active Earth Pressure Coefficient Ka:
Ka = tan²(45° - φ/2) = (1 - sin 32°) / (1 + sin 32°) = 0.3073

2. Upper Dry Layer (h1 = 4 ft):
• Effective stress at GWT: σ'v1 = 110 × 4 = 440 psf
• Lateral thrust Pa1 = 0.5 × Ka × γ × h1² = 0.5 × 0.3073 × 110 × 16 = 270.4 lb/ft
• Lever arm above toe: y1 = hw + h1/3 = 4 + 1.333 = 5.333 ft
• Overturning moment M1 = 270.4 × 5.333 = 1,442.1 ft-lb/ft

3. Submerged Layer (hw = 4 ft, γ' = 125 - 62.4 = 62.6 pcf):
• Surcharge from dry soil: Pa2,rect = Ka × (γ × h1) × hw = 0.3073 × 440 × 4 = 540.8 lb/ft
  Arm y2,rect = hw / 2 = 2.0 ft → M2,rect = 540.8 × 2.0 = 1,081.6 ft-lb/ft
• Triangular Submerged Soil Thrust: Pa2,tri = 0.5 × Ka × γ' × hw² = 0.5 × 0.3073 × 62.6 × 16 = 153.9 lb/ft
  Arm y2,tri = hw / 3 = 1.333 ft → M2,tri = 153.9 × 1.333 = 205.2 ft-lb/ft

4. Hydrostatic Pore Water Pressure Thrust (Pw):
• Max pore pressure at base: u_base = γw × hw = 62.4 × 4 = 249.6 psf
• Hydrostatic thrust Pw = 0.5 × γw × hw² = 0.5 × 62.4 × 16 = 499.2 lb/ft
• Arm yw = hw / 3 = 1.333 ft → Mw = 499.2 × 1.333 = 665.6 ft-lb/ft

5. Total Overturning Moment MOT:
MOT = 1,442.1 + 1,081.6 + 205.2 + 665.6 = 3,394.5 ft-lb/ft

6. Resisting Moment ΣMR (same concrete wall sections as Problem 96):
• W1 = 0.5 × 2 × 8 × 150 = 1,200 lb, arm = ⅔ × 2 = 1.333 ft → MR1 = 1,600 ft-lb
• W2 = 2 × 8 × 150 = 2,400 lb, arm = 2 + 1 = 3.0 ft → MR2 = 7,200 ft-lb
• ΣMR = 1,600 + 7,200 = 8,800 ft-lb/ft

7. Factor of Safety against Overturning (FS_OT):
FS_OT = ΣMR / MOT = 8,800 / 3,394.5 = 2.59 (Rounds to 2.6)
shortcut:
Notice the dramatic effect of pore water pressure! In Problem 96 (dry backfill), FS was 3.1. When water fills the lower 4 ft, hydrostatic pore water pressure pushes directly with Ka = 1.0 (water exerts isotropic fluid pressure), reducing the safety factor from 3.1 to 2.6.

Quick Check Rule:
Hydrostatic water force alone is Pw = 0.5 × 62.4 × hw² = 31.2 × hw².
Always remember: below the water table, use the buoyant unit weight (γ' = γsat - 62.4) for effective soil pressure, and then ADD the full hydrostatic pore water pressure (γw) separately!
fifthGrader:
Think of what happens when you soak dirt behind a wall with water. Water is heavy and pushes outward like a swimming pool against the back of the concrete wall.

Because water has no friction to hold itself together, it pushes with 100% of its fluid force! This extra pore water push makes the wall tip much more easily, dropping our factor of safety from 3.1 down to 2.6.

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect: 2.1 occurs if you mistakenly use the full saturated unit weight (γsat = 125 pcf) below the water table without subtracting the unit weight of water (buoyant unit weight γ' = γsat - 62.4 = 62.6 pcf).

options.label: B
options.feedback: ✓ Correct! ΣMR = 8,800 ft-lb/ft, MOT = 3,394.5 ft-lb/ft (including 665.6 ft-lb/ft from hydrostatic pore water pressure), giving FS_OT = 8,800 / 3,394.5 = 2.59 ≈ 2.6.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect: 3.1 is the safety factor for the completely dry wall from Problem 96. Neglecting the submerged pore water pressure gives an unsafely unconservative estimate!

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect: Check your moment calculation about toe Point O and ensure pore water pressure Pw = 0.5 * γw * hw² acts at hw/3.

title: Planar Slope Stability (c-φ Soil Failure Surface)
description:
A cutting in a hillside exposes an assumed planar slip surface inclined at an angle αs = 28° to the horizontal with an assumed slip length Ls = 36 ft. The total weight of the active sliding soil wedge above the slip plane is WM = 85,000 lb/ft (85 kips/ft).

The soil possesses an apparent cohesion c = 250 psf and an angle of internal friction φ = 24°. Neglect pore water pressure.

Using limit equilibrium analysis along a planar failure surface, the factor of safety (FS) against slope instability is most nearly:
hint:
1. Mobilized Shear Force (Driving Force TMOB):
TMOB = WM × sin(αs) = 85,000 × sin(28°) = 85,000 × 0.4695 = 39,905 lb/ft

2. Normal Force on Slip Surface (N):
N = WM × cos(αs) = 85,000 × cos(28°) = 85,000 × 0.8829 = 75,051 lb/ft

3. Available Shearing Resistance (TFF):
TFF = c × Ls + N × tan(φ)
• Cohesive force = 250 psf × 36 ft = 9,000 lb/ft
• Frictional force = 75,051 × tan(24°) = 75,051 × 0.4452 = 33,415 lb/ft
• TFF = 9,000 + 33,415 = 42,415 lb/ft

4. Factor of Safety (FS):
FS = TFF / TMOB = 42,415 / 39,905 = 1.0629 ≈ 1.06
shortcut:
Remember the fundamental force balance:
• Driving downslope: WM × sin(α)
• Normal clamping: WM × cos(α)
• Resistance: c × Ls + (WM × cos(α)) × tan(φ)
FS = [c·Ls + WM·cos(α)·tan(φ)] / [WM·sin(α)]
With FS = 1.06, this slope is in a state of marginal equilibrium near impending failure (FS ~ 1.0).
fifthGrader:
Imagine you build a giant pile of wet sand at the beach. If you pile it up way too steeply, a big chunk of it suddenly slides down onto your feet.

That slide happens because gravity is pulling the sand downward like a playground slide, while the sand particles sticking together are trying to hold hands and stay put. Engineers use a score called the Factor of Safety to measure this. It compares the forces fighting to keep the hill stable against the forces trying to make it slide. If the 'staying put' forces win by a lot, the hill is safe. If gravity wins, down comes the dirt!

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect: 0.84 is the inverse ratio TMOB / TFF. Factor of safety is resisting capacity divided by mobilized demand: FS = TFF / TMOB.

options.label: B
options.feedback: ✓ Correct! Driving force TMOB = 85,000 × sin(28°) = 39,905 lb/ft. Resisting force TFF = (250 × 36) + (85,000 × cos(28°) × tan(24°)) = 42,415 lb/ft. Yielding FS = 42,415 / 39,905 = 1.06.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect: Be sure not to invert sin(α) and cos(α). Normal force is WM·cos(α) and driving shear is WM·sin(α).

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect: Check your cohesive resistance term. Cohesion c must be integrated across the entire slip surface length Ls (c × Ls = 250 × 36 = 9,000 lb/ft).

title: Cohesionless Granular Slope & Angle of Repose (c = 0)
description:
An infinite slope constructed of clean granular gravelly sand has an internal friction angle φ = 34° and zero cohesion (c = 0). The slope is inclined at an angle αs = 25° to the horizontal. An assumed planar failure surface runs parallel to the ground surface at length Ls = 50 ft with a total soil wedge weight WM = 140,000 lb/ft.

Under dry conditions, the factor of safety (FS) against slope instability is most nearly:
hint:
1. For a purely cohesionless soil (c = 0):
TFF = 0 + WM × cos(αs) × tan(φ)
TMOB = WM × sin(αs)

2. Compute Factor of Safety:
FS = TFF / TMOB = [WM × cos(αs) × tan(φ)] / [WM × sin(αs)]
FS = tan(φ) / tan(αs)

3. Evaluate with φ = 34° and αs = 25°:
tan(34°) = 0.6745
tan(25°) = 0.4663
FS = 0.6745 / 0.4663 = 1.4465 ≈ 1.45
shortcut:
⚡ NCEES Exam Golden Shortcut for Cohesionless Slopes (c = 0):
Neither the soil weight WM, slip length Ls, nor thickness matter!
FS = tan(φ) / tan(αs)
If αs < φ, the slope is stable (FS > 1.0). The maximum angle the slope can sustain before sliding is called the angle of repose (αs = φ).
fifthGrader: Think of pouring dry sand out of a bucket into a cone. You can only make the cone so steep before extra sand just tumbles down the sides. That's because dry sand has no glue (cohesion) between the grains—only the rough friction of rocks rubbing together holds it up. If the hill is flatter than the sand's natural friction angle, it stays put with a great safety score of 1.45!

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect: 0.69 is tan(25°) / tan(34°). FS is friction capacity over slope demand: FS = tan(φ) / tan(αs).

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect: Don't take the direct angle ratio (34° / 25° = 1.36) or subtract angles. The trigonometric tangents must be evaluated: tan(34°) / tan(25°) = 1.45.

options.label: C
options.feedback: ✓ Correct! For any cohesionless slope (c = 0), soil weight cancels out: FS = tan(φ) / tan(αs) = tan(34°) / tan(25°) = 0.6745 / 0.4663 = 1.45.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect: Review the ratio of available friction to mobilized driving shear.

title: Planar Slope Stability with Seepage & Pore Water Pressure
description:
A hillside slope has a planar slip surface inclined at αs = 30° to the horizontal with a slip length Ls = 40 ft. The sliding soil wedge weight is WM = 120,000 lb/ft. The soil has cohesion c = 200 psf and friction angle φ = 30°.

Following a severe torrential rainstorm, groundwater seepage develops along the slip surface, generating an upward pore water force (hydraulic uplift) U = 35,000 lb/ft acting normal to the slip surface.

The factor of safety (FS) against slope instability during this storm event is most nearly:
hint:
1. Mobilized Shear Force (Driving):
TMOB = WM × sin(αs) = 120,000 × sin(30°) = 120,000 × 0.50 = 60,000 lb/ft

2. Effective Normal Force with Pore Water Uplift (N'):
Total normal force N = WM × cos(αs) = 120,000 × cos(30°) = 103,923 lb/ft
Effective normal force N' = N - U = 103,923 - 35,000 = 68,923 lb/ft

3. Available Shearing Resistance (TFF):
• Cohesion force = c × Ls = 200 psf × 40 ft = 8,000 lb/ft
• Frictional force = N' × tan(φ) = 68,923 × tan(30°) = 68,923 × 0.57735 = 39,793 lb/ft
• TFF = 8,000 + 39,793 = 47,793 lb/ft

4. Factor of Safety (FS):
FS = TFF / TMOB = 47,793 / 60,000 = 0.7966 ≈ 0.80
(Since FS < 1.0, active slope failure occurs!)
shortcut: Notice the dangerous power of pore water pressure! Under dry conditions, N was 103,923 lb/ft giving FS = 68,000 / 60,000 = 1.13. But seepage pore pressure acts like hydraulic jacks pushing upward along the slip plane, lowering clamping pressure to 68,923 lb/ft. This causes FS to plummet from 1.13 down to 0.80—causing a landslide!
fifthGrader:
Think of sliding down a plastic slip-and-slide! When it's dry, you stick to the plastic because of friction. But when someone turns on the garden hose, the water gets between you and the ground and lifts you up just enough that you go zooming down fast!

That's exactly what rainwater does inside a hill: the water pushes upward along the crack, reduces the friction holding the dirt, and causes a landslide!

options.label: A
options.feedback: ✓ Correct! Hydraulic uplift reduces effective normal force to N' = 120,000·cos(30°) - 35,000 = 68,923 lb/ft. Available resistance TFF = (200 × 40) + 68,923·tan(30°) = 47,793 lb/ft. FS = 47,793 / 60,000 = 0.80 (Slope failure).

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect: 1.00 represents critical equilibrium. With U = 35,000 lb/ft, the driving force exceeds resisting strength.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect: 1.13 is the dry slope factor of safety without pore water pressure (U = 0). Always subtract pore water uplift U from normal force N.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect: Do not add pore water force to normal force. Pore water pressure acts as an uplift that reduces effective stress.

title: Slope Remediation: Required Cohesion for Design FS = 1.50
description:
An embankment excavation requires a factor of safety FS = 1.50 against planar slope failure to meet DOT highway specifications. The assumed planar slip surface is inclined at αs = 32° to the horizontal with length Ls = 45 ft. The sliding soil wedge weight is WM = 110,000 lb/ft. The soil has an internal friction angle φ = 22°. Neglect pore water pressure.

To achieve the target factor of safety of 1.50 (for example via soil bio-reinforcement or cement grouting), the required apparent soil cohesion (creq) is most nearly:
hint:
1. Driving Mobilized Shear Force (TMOB):
TMOB = WM × sin(αs) = 110,000 × sin(32°) = 110,000 × 0.5299 = 58,291 lb/ft

2. Required Available Shear Resistance for FS = 1.50:
FS = TFF,req / TMOB  →  TFF,req = 1.50 × 58,291 = 87,437 lb/ft

3. Frictional Resistance Provided by Soil (Tfric):
N = WM × cos(αs) = 110,000 × cos(32°) = 110,000 × 0.8480 = 93,285 lb/ft
Tfric = N × tan(φ) = 93,285 × tan(22°) = 93,285 × 0.4040 = 37,690 lb/ft

4. Required Cohesive Resistance (Tcoh,req):
TFF,req = Tcoh,req + Tfric
Tcoh,req = 87,437 - 37,690 = 49,747 lb/ft

5. Solve for Required Cohesion creq:
Tcoh,req = creq × Ls
creq = 49,747 lb/ft / 45 ft = 1,105.5 psf ≈ 1,110 psf
shortcut:
Back-calculation formula:
creq = [FS × WM·sin(αs) - WM·cos(αs)·tan(φ)] / Ls
creq = [1.50 × 58,291 - 37,690] / 45 = 49,747 / 45 = 1,105.5 psf (Rounds to 1,110 psf).

You know how much friction the sand already has, so you calculate how much 'glue' or plant roots (cohesion) you need to add to reach that safety score: exactly 1,110 pounds of stickiness per square foot!

title: Wood Retaining Wall: Post Sizing, Embedment Depth & Bending Stress in Sand
description:
A cantilever wood post-and-lagging retaining wall is designed to retain a sandy backfill to an exposed height H = 6.0 ft. Vertical square timber posts are installed at a center-to-center spacing S = 4.0 ft. The ground surface behind the wall carries a uniform surcharge q = 100 psf.

The retained granular backfill and foundation sand have an internal friction angle φ = 32°, cohesion c = 0, and total unit weight γ = 115 pcf. The backfill is well-drained with no water table (pore water pressure u = 0). The allowable timber bending stress is F'b = 1,350 psi.

Using Rankine active earth pressure theory, determine:
1. The maximum bending moment M_grade at the ground line for a 6×6 post (dressed 5.5" × 5.5"), and whether it passes in flexure.
2. The minimum required timber post size (from 4×4 up to 12×12) that satisfies the allowable bending stress.
3. The geotechnical embedment depth D required to anchor the post against lateral earth pressure (using soldier pile limit equilibrium where D ≈ 1.0 to 1.1 × H).

The maximum bending stress in a 6×6 post and the minimum acceptable standard timber post size are most nearly:
hint:
1. Rankine Active Earth Pressure Coefficient Ka:
Ka = tan²(45° - φ/2) = (1 - sin 32°) / (1 + sin 32°) = 0.3073

2. Lateral Soil Active Thrust (per linear foot of wall):
• Pa,soil = 0.5 × Ka × γ × H² = 0.5 × 0.3073 × 115 × 6.0² = 636.1 lb/ft
• Lever arm above base: y_soil = H / 3 = 6.0 / 3 = 2.0 ft
• M_soil = Pa,soil × y_soil = 636.1 × 2.0 = 1,272.2 ft-lb/ft

3. Surcharge Lateral Thrust (per linear foot of wall):
• P_q = Ka × q × H = 0.3073 × 100 × 6.0 = 184.4 lb/ft
• Lever arm above base: y_q = H / 2 = 6.0 / 2 = 3.0 ft
• M_q = P_q × y_q = 184.4 × 3.0 = 553.1 ft-lb/ft

4. Total Base Overturning Moment & Tributary Load per Post (S = 4.0 ft):
• Total lateral load per post: P_post = (Pa,soil + P_q) × S = (636.1 + 184.4) × 4.0 = 3,282 lb
• Total base moment per post: M_grade = (M_soil + M_q) × S = (1,272.2 + 553.1) × 4.0 = 7,301.2 ft-lb (87,614 in-lb)

5. Flexural Stress Check for 6×6 Post:
• Dressed dimensions: b = d = 5.5 in
• Section Modulus: Sx = (b × d²) / 6 = (5.5 × 5.5²) / 6 = 27.73 in³
• Actual bending stress: fb = (M_grade × 12) / Sx = 87,614 / 27.73 = 3,159 psi
• Since fb = 3,159 psi > F'b = 1,350 psi, the 6×6 post is severely OVERSTRESSED (Stress ratio = 2.34) → FAILS!

6. Determine Minimum Acceptable Post Size:
• Required Sx,min = (M_grade × 12) / F'b = 87,614 / 1,350 = 64.90 in³
• 4×4: Sx = 7.15 in³ (Fails)
• 6×6: Sx = 27.73 in³ (Fails)
• 8×8 (dressed 7.5" × 7.5"): Sx = (7.5³) / 6 = 70.31 in³ > 64.90 in³ → PASSES! (fb = 1,246 psi, Stress ratio = 0.92)
• Therefore, an 8×8 post is the minimum acceptable standard size.

7. Embedment Depth ("How Deep to Dig"):
• For isolated cantilever soldier piles in cohesionless sand (φ = 32°), taking Broms' limit equilibrium with passive resistance over effective width b_eff = 3b yields a required embedment D_req ≈ 1.05 to 1.10 × H ≈ 6.3 to 6.6 ft.
• Standard practice specifies digging D ≥ 6.5 ft into competent sand.
shortcut:
Rule of Thumb for Timber Retaining Walls:
1. Flexure Governing: For cantilever walls higher than 4.5 ft with typical 4 ft to 6 ft spacing, 4×4 and 6×6 posts almost always fail in bending! A 6 ft high wall with surcharge requires at least an 8×8 post.
2. Embedment Depth ("How Deep to Dig"): For granular sand, dig depth D must be at least equal to exposed height H (D ≥ H). Here, H = 6 ft means D must be at least 6.5 ft.
3. Common Trap: Do not use nominal 6" × 6" dimensions (Sx = 6³/6 = 36 in³). Always use actual dressed dimensions (5.5" × 5.5", Sx = 27.73 in³)! Using nominal dimensions underestimates bending stress by 30%!
fifthGrader:
Think of the vertical wood post like a giant ruler clamped at the bottom in the dirt, with a bucket of dirt and rocks pushing hard against the top 6 feet.

A skinny 4x4 or 6x6 post will bend and snap like a twig under 3,280 pounds of soil push (creating 3,160 psi of stress against an allowable 1,350 psi limit)!

To hold back 6 feet of dirt safely, you must upgrade to an 8x8 timber post, and you have to bury the post just as deep into the ground as it sticks out into the air (dig at least 6.5 feet deep) so the dirt doesn't yank it out!

title: Wood Retaining Wall in Saturated Silt: Severe Pore Water Pressure & Embedment
description:
A cantilever wood retaining wall using 8×8 timber posts (dressed 7.5" × 7.5") spaced at S = 5.0 ft retains H = 6.0 ft of fine silty soil. The silt has an internal friction angle φ = 26°, cohesion c = 0, moist unit weight γ = 110 pcf, and saturated unit weight γsat = 125 pcf.

Due to absent or clogged weep holes after extended rainfall, the water table rises to a height hw = 4.0 ft above the ground line (unit weight of water γw = 62.4 pcf). No surcharge acts on the surface.

Account for effective soil stress with buoyant unit weight γ' = γsat - γw and full hydrostatic pore water pressure u = γw × hw. Neglect wall friction.

The total overturning moment M_grade at the ground line per post and the required dig depth D into the silt (where poor drainage and high pore pressure demand D ≈ 1.35 × H) are most nearly:
hint:
1. Rankine Active Earth Pressure Coefficient Ka for Silt (φ = 26°):
Ka = tan²(45° - 26°/2) = (1 - sin 26°) / (1 + sin 26°) = (1 - 0.4384) / (1 + 0.4384) = 0.3904

2. Soil Geometry & Strata:
• Dry upper silt layer: h_dry = H - hw = 6.0 - 4.0 = 2.0 ft
• Submerged silt layer: hw = 4.0 ft
• Buoyant unit weight: γ' = γsat - γw = 125 - 62.4 = 62.6 pcf

3. Lateral Forces per Linear Foot of Wall:
(a) Upper dry silt layer (h_dry = 2 ft):
• Pa1 = 0.5 × Ka × γ × h_dry² = 0.5 × 0.3904 × 110 × 2² = 85.9 lb/ft
• Arm y1 = hw + (h_dry / 3) = 4.0 + 0.667 = 4.667 ft
• M1 = 85.9 × 4.667 = 400.9 ft-lb/ft

(b) Overburden surcharge from dry silt on lower submerged layer:
• q_dry = γ × h_dry = 110 × 2.0 = 220 psf
• Pa2,rect = Ka × q_dry × hw = 0.3904 × 220 × 4.0 = 343.6 lb/ft
• Arm y2,rect = hw / 2 = 2.0 ft
• M2,rect = 343.6 × 2.0 = 687.2 ft-lb/ft

(c) Submerged effective silt thrust (buoyant):
• Pa2,tri = 0.5 × Ka × γ' × hw² = 0.5 × 0.3904 × 62.6 × 4.0² = 195.5 lb/ft
• Arm y2,tri = hw / 3 = 4.0 / 3 = 1.333 ft
• M2,tri = 195.5 × 1.333 = 260.6 ft-lb/ft

(d) Hydrostatic Pore Water Pressure Thrust (Pw):
• Max pore pressure at base: u_base = γw × hw = 62.4 × 4.0 = 249.6 psf
• Pw = 0.5 × γw × hw² = 0.5 × 62.4 × 16 = 499.2 lb/ft
• Arm yw = hw / 3 = 1.333 ft
• Mw = 499.2 × 1.333 = 665.4 ft-lb/ft

4. Total Overturning Moment per Linear Foot:
• M_base,total = M1 + M2,rect + M2,tri + Mw = 400.9 + 687.2 + 260.6 + 665.4 = 2,014.1 ft-lb/ft

5. Total Base Overturning Moment per Post (Spacing S = 5.0 ft):
• M_grade = M_base,total × S = 2,014.1 × 5.0 = 10,070.5 ft-lb ≈ 10,071 ft-lb

6. Required Embedment Depth in Saturated Silt:
• Because of high pore water pressure and low passive resistance in saturated silt, embedment depth requires D ≈ 1.35 × H = 1.35 × 6.0 = 8.1 ft (at least 8.0 ft dug depth).
shortcut:
Pore Water Pressure is the #1 Cause of Retaining Wall Failures!
Notice that pore water pressure alone creates Pw = 499.2 lb/ft and Mw = 665.4 ft-lb/ft—accounting for over 33% of the total overturning torque on the wall! Installing a 4-inch perforated drain pipe with crushed rock backfill completely relieves this hydrostatic pressure, reducing the base moment from 10,071 ft-lb down to 6,743 ft-lb (a 33% reduction) and allowing significantly shallower post dig depth!
fifthGrader:
When rain fills up dirt like a wet sponge behind a wooden wall, the water pushes with massive force straight against the boards. Water doesn't have any friction to hold itself up, so it acts like a giant liquid battering ram.

This extra water pressure increases the tipping torque on each post to over 10,000 ft-lb! To keep the posts from tilting over, you must dig the post hole down 8 feet deep into the ground—deeper than the wall is tall!

title: Low Cantilever Wood Wall in Cohesive Clay: 4×4 vs 6×6 Post Sizing & Embedment
description:
A low garden terrace retaining wall of exposed height H = 4.0 ft is built using timber posts spaced at S = 3.0 ft. The wall retains and is embedded into a stiff cohesive clay with undrained shear strength c = 600 psf, internal friction angle φ = 0°, and unit weight γ = 110 pcf. No water table is present.

According to Rankine cohesive earth pressure theory, active pressure for φ = 0 is σa = γ·z - 2c. Tension cracks can develop to depth z0 = 2c/γ = 2(600)/110 = 10.9 ft > H. However, per geotechnical retaining wall standards, to prevent unsafe design when tension cracks fill with rainwater or clay desiccates, design active pressure is taken as an equivalent fluid pressure with equivalent fluid weight γeq = 40 pcf.

The allowable timber bending stress is F'b = 1,350 psi.

Determine whether a standard 4×4 post (dressed 3.5" × 3.5") is adequate, or if a 6×6 post (dressed 5.5" × 5.5") is required, and determine the maximum bending stress fb in the 4×4 post:
hint:
1. Equivalent Fluid Active Lateral Thrust (per linear foot of wall):
• Equivalent fluid unit weight: γeq = 40 pcf
• Pa = 0.5 × γeq × H² = 0.5 × 40 × 4.0² = 320.0 lb/ft
• Lever arm above base: y = H / 3 = 4.0 / 3 = 1.333 ft
• Overturning moment per foot: M_base = 320.0 × 1.333 = 426.7 ft-lb/ft

2. Base Shear and Moment per Post (Spacing S = 3.0 ft):
• P_post = Pa × S = 320.0 × 3.0 = 960.0 lb
• M_grade = M_base × S = 426.7 × 3.0 = 1,280.0 ft-lb (15,360 in-lb)

3. Check 4×4 Wood Post:
• Dressed dimensions: b = d = 3.5 in
• Section modulus Sx = (3.5 × 3.5²) / 6 = 7.15 in³
• Actual bending stress: fb = (M_grade × 12) / Sx = 15,360 / 7.15 = 2,148 psi
• Since fb = 2,148 psi > F'b = 1,350 psi (Stress ratio = 1.59), the 4×4 post FAILS in bending!

4. Check 6×6 Wood Post:
• Dressed dimensions: b = d = 5.5 in
• Section modulus Sx = (5.5³) / 6 = 27.73 in³
• Actual bending stress: fb = 15,360 / 27.73 = 554 psi
• Since fb = 554 psi < F'b = 1,350 psi (Stress ratio = 0.41), the 6×6 post PASSES with generous margin of safety!

5. Required Dig Depth in Clay:
• Using Broms' method for cohesive soil, required embedment D ≈ 1.0 to 1.15 × H ≈ 4.5 ft to anchor the post against lateral kickout in stiff clay.
shortcut:
The 4×4 Retaining Wall Trap:
Homeowners and DIYers frequently try to build 4-ft retaining walls using 4×4 posts. Even for a short 4-ft wall with close 3-ft spacing, a 4×4 experiences 2,148 psi—exceeding its allowable limit by nearly 60%! The wall will tilt and fail within 1 to 2 seasons. A 6×6 post is structurally mandatory for walls taller than 3 feet.
fifthGrader:
Lots of people try to use 4x4 fence posts to build backyard garden walls, thinking 4 feet isn't very tall. But 4 feet of heavy wet clay pushes with nearly 1,000 pounds of force on every post!

The 4x4 post bends under 2,150 psi of bending stress—way past the 1,350 psi safety limit. It will crack or lean over. You must use at least a thick 6x6 post, dug 4.5 feet deep into the clay!

title: Heavy Timber Cantilever Wall Socketed into Rock with Highway Surcharge
description:
A heavy-duty timber cantilever wall retains H = 8.0 ft of granular backfill (φ = 34°, c = 0, γ = 120 pcf) adjacent to a commercial access road carrying an AASHTO vehicular surcharge q = 250 psf (equivalent to 2 ft of soil overburden). Timber posts are spaced at S = 6.0 ft on center.

The wall is founded on and socketed into competent bedrock. In solid rock, allowable lateral bearing resistance is extremely high, allowing the post embedment depth to be governed by rock socketing (D_req ≈ 0.40 to 0.50 × H, min 3.0 ft).

The allowable bending stress for selected heavy timber posts is F'b = 1,450 psi.

Evaluate the required post size (comparing 8×8, 10×10, and 12×12 square timber posts) and determine the maximum bending moment M_grade per post and the minimum post size that safely carries this moment:
hint:
1. Rankine Active Earth Pressure Coefficient Ka for Sand Backfill (φ = 34°):
Ka = tan²(45° - 34°/2) = (1 - sin 34°) / (1 + sin 34°) = (1 - 0.5592) / (1 + 0.5592) = 0.2827

2. Lateral Soil Active Thrust (per linear foot of wall):
• Pa,soil = 0.5 × Ka × γ × H² = 0.5 × 0.2827 × 120 × 8.0² = 1,085.6 lb/ft
• Arm y_soil = H / 3 = 8.0 / 3 = 2.667 ft
• M_soil = 1,085.6 × 2.667 = 2,895.0 ft-lb/ft

3. Vehicular Surcharge Thrust (per linear foot of wall):
• P_q = Ka × q × H = 0.2827 × 250 × 8.0 = 565.4 lb/ft
• Arm y_q = H / 2 = 8.0 / 2 = 4.0 ft
• M_q = 565.4 × 4.0 = 2,261.6 ft-lb/ft

4. Total Base Overturning Moment per Post (Spacing S = 6.0 ft):
• M_base,total = M_soil + M_q = 2,895.0 + 2,261.6 = 5,156.6 ft-lb/ft
• Total moment per post: M_grade = 5,156.6 × 6.0 = 30,939.6 ft-lb (371,275 in-lb)

5. Minimum Required Section Modulus Sx,min:
• Sx,min = (M_grade × 12) / F'b = 371,275 / 1,450 = 256.0 in³

6. Compare Standard Heavy Timber Post Sizes:
• 8×8 (dressed 7.5" × 7.5"): Sx = 70.31 in³ (fb = 5,280 psi >> 1,450 psi → FAILS)
• 10×10 (dressed 9.5" × 9.5"): Sx = (9.5³) / 6 = 142.9 in³ (fb = 2,598 psi > 1,450 psi → FAILS)
• 12×12 (dressed 11.5" × 11.5"): Sx = (11.5³) / 6 = 253.3 in³ ≈ 256 in³ (fb = 1,465 psi ≈ 1,450 psi, within 1% of allowable)
• If S is tightened slightly to 5.5 ft or a 12×12 select structural timber is used, 12×12 is the only standard post size capable of resisting this massive 30,940 ft-lb moment!

7. Rock Socket Embedment Depth:
• In sound bedrock, lateral resistance is governed by rock crushing strength rather than soil yielding. A socket depth of D ≈ 0.40 to 0.45 × H = 3.2 to 3.5 ft (min 3 ft) provides full base fixity.
shortcut:
The Limits of Cantilever Timber Walls:
An 8-ft cantilever retaining wall with highway traffic and wide 6-ft spacing generates over 30,900 ft-lb of bending moment on each post! Even massive 10×10 timbers fail in bending. Only a 12×12 heavy timber (or reducing post spacing S to 4 ft) can carry this load without tieback anchors or deadmen. Meanwhile, because the foundation is solid rock, the required embedment depth is only ~3.5 ft, showing that bedrock dramatically reduces dig depth while timber flexure becomes the critical governing limit!
fifthGrader:
When heavy semi-trucks drive right next to an 8-foot-high wall, the pushing force against the wood is enormous—over 30,900 foot-pounds of torque per post!

Even an 8x8 or 10x10 tree trunk will snap in half under this pressure. You need a colossal 12x12 solid timber post!

However, because the ground is solid bedrock, you only need to drill 3.5 feet deep into the rock to anchor it tight!

title: Cantilever Wood Wall: Horizontal Timber Lagging Thickness & Soil Arching
description:
A cantilever wood post-and-lagging retaining wall retains granular backfill to an exposed height H = 8.0 ft. Vertical timber posts are installed at a center-to-center spacing S = 5.0 ft. The retained backfill has an internal friction angle φ = 34°, cohesion c = 0, and unit weight γ = 120 pcf. A uniform traffic surcharge q = 150 psf acts on the horizontal ground surface behind the wall.

Horizontal timber lagging planks span between the posts to retain the soil. According to AASHTO and FHWA Geotechnical Circular GEC No. 4 guidelines for flexible soldier pile lagging, soil arching behind the boards redistributes lateral earth pressure toward the stiffer vertical posts, allowing the maximum design bending moment in the lagging to be calculated as:

M_max = (p_max · S²) / 10

where p_max is the maximum lateral earth pressure (psf) acting at the bottom of the wall (z = H), and S is the center-to-center post spacing.

The allowable timber bending stress for rough/dressed lagging boards in wet service conditions is F'b = 1,200 psi. Standard nominal timber plank sizes are:
• 2-inch nominal (dressed actual thickness t = 1.5 in.)
• 3-inch nominal (dressed actual thickness t = 2.5 in.)
• 4-inch nominal (dressed actual thickness t = 3.5 in.)

Determine the maximum lateral pressure p_max at the base of the wall, the maximum lagging bending moment M_max per foot of wall height, and the minimum standard nominal lagging thickness required to safely carry this moment:
hint:
1. Rankine Active Earth Pressure Coefficient Ka:
Ka = tan²(45° - φ/2) = (1 - sin 34°) / (1 + sin 34°) = (1 - 0.5592) / (1 + 0.5592) = 0.2827

2. Maximum Lateral Earth Pressure at Base (z = H = 8.0 ft):
• Total vertical effective stress at base: σv = γ · H + q = (120 × 8.0) + 150 = 960 + 150 = 1,110 psf
• Maximum lateral active pressure: p_max = Ka × σv = 0.2827 × 1,110 = 313.8 psf

3. Maximum Bending Moment in Lagging with Soil Arching (AASHTO / FHWA):
• Due to soil arching behind flexible boards, the simple beam moment (p S² / 8) is reduced by 20% to (p S² / 10):
• M_max = (p_max × S²) / 10 = (313.8 × 5.0²) / 10 = (313.8 × 25) / 10 = 784.5 ft-lb per linear foot of wall height
• In inch-pounds: M_max = 784.5 × 12 = 9,414 in-lb/ft

4. Required Section Modulus Sx,req per Foot of Height (b = 12 in.):
• Sx,req = M_max / F'b = 9,414 / 1,200 = 7.845 in³/ft ≈ 7.85 in³/ft

5. Evaluate Standard Timber Lagging Plank Sizes:
• For a 12-inch strip of plank with actual thickness t:
  Sx = (b × t²) / 6 = (12 × t²) / 6 = 2 × t² in³/ft

(a) 2" Nominal (t = 1.5 in.):
  Sx = 2 × (1.5)² = 4.50 in³/ft < 7.85 in³/ft → FAILS!
  Actual bending stress: fb = 9,414 / 4.50 = 2,092 psi > 1,200 psi (Overstressed by 74%!)

(b) 3" Nominal (t = 2.5 in.):
  Sx = 2 × (2.5)² = 12.50 in³/ft > 7.85 in³/ft → PASSES!
  Actual bending stress: fb = 9,414 / 12.50 = 753 psi < 1,200 psi (Safe, utilization = 63%)

(c) 4" Nominal (t = 3.5 in.):
  Sx = 2 × (3.5)² = 24.50 in³/ft >> 7.85 in³/ft (Overkill for this span)

• Conclusion: 3-inch nominal timber lagging is the minimum acceptable standard size.

Soil Arching in Retaining Walls:
1. Simple Beam Trap: If you forget soil arching and use M = p S² / 8, M = 313.8 × 25 / 8 = 980.6 ft-lb (Sx,req = 9.81 in³). Although 3-inch lagging is still required, using S²/8 significantly over-engineers the lumber.
2. Rapid Lagging Formula: For a 1-ft wide plank strip, Sx = 2 · t². Setting 2 · t² ≥ M_in-lb / F'b gives t_req = sqrt(M_in-lb / (2 · F'b)). Here, t_req = sqrt(9,414 / 2,400) = sqrt(3.92) = 1.98 in. Since 2" nominal is only 1.5" thick, you immediately know you must step up to 3" nominal (2.5" actual)!
fifthGrader:
Imagine horizontal wooden planks held at each end by thick posts 5 feet apart, holding back an 8-foot pile of heavy sand.

Down at the very bottom, the dirt pushes the hardest—over 314 pounds on every square foot of wood!

If you use thin 2-inch boards (which are really only 1.5 inches thick), the dirt push will bow and snap the boards right in the middle.

To hold the dirt without breaking, you need thick 3-inch planks (2.5 inches thick)!

title: Shallow Dig Depth Engineering: Sizing an Augered Concrete Pier (Broms & IBC)
description:
A cantilever wood post-and-lagging retaining wall retains granular sand to an exposed height H = 6.0 ft. Vertical square 8×8 timber posts (dressed 7.5" × 7.5") are installed at center-to-center spacing S = 4.0 ft. The retained backfill has internal friction angle φ = 32°, cohesion c = 0, and unit weight γ = 115 pcf. Surcharge q = 100 psf acts on the surface.

The total active earth thrust per post is P_post = 3,282 lb, acting at lever arm h = 2.23 ft above the ground line (base moment M_grade = 7,301 ft-lb). The passive earth pressure coefficient of the foundation sand is Kp = tan²(45° + 32°/2) = 3.255.

Due to shallow underground fiber-optic and electrical utilities at the property line, the maximum allowable excavation depth for post foundations is strictly capped at D_max = 4.5 ft. Direct burial of an isolated timber post (b = 7.5 in. = 0.625 ft) requires an embedment depth D ≈ 6.5 ft, violating the 4.5 ft site restriction.

To safely satisfy the shallow 4.5 ft excavation limit without deadman tiebacks, the engineer specifies augering a cylindrical hole and encasing the post in a 3,000 psi concrete pier.

Using Broms' limit equilibrium method for a short rigid pier in cohesionless sand (where allowable lateral moment resistance with safety factor is M_all = 0.5 · Kp · γ · b · D³), determine the minimum standard auger diameter b (from 12-inch, 16-inch, 20-inch, 24-inch) required to achieve full stability at D = 4.5 ft:
hint:
1. Understand the Shallow Dig Constraint:
• Maximum allowable excavation depth: D_max = 4.5 ft
• Applied lateral load per post: P_post = 3,282 lb
• Load lever arm above grade: h = 2.23 ft

2. Overturning Moment about Base of Pier (D = 4.5 ft):
• Total moment lever arm from top of thrust to base of pier: L_arm = h + D = 2.23 + 4.5 = 6.73 ft
• Total overturning moment: M_OT = P_post × (h + D) = 3,282 × 6.73 = 22,088 ft-lb

3. Broms' Allowable Passive Moment Resistance Capacity:
• Kp = tan²(45° + 32°/2) = (1 + sin 32°) / (1 - sin 32°) = 1.5299 / 0.4701 = 3.255
• M_all = 0.5 × Kp × γ × b × D³
• For D = 4.5 ft, D³ = (4.5)³ = 91.125 ft³
• M_all = 0.5 × 3.255 × 115 × b × 91.125 = 17,055 × b ft-lb (where b is pier diameter in feet)

4. Solve for Required Pier Diameter b:
• Equating M_all ≥ M_OT:
  17,055 × b ≥ 22,088
  b_min = 22,088 / 17,055 = 1.295 ft
• In inches: b_min = 1.295 × 12 = 15.54 inches

5. Compare Standard Auger Sizes:
• 12-inch auger (b = 1.0 ft): M_all = 17,055 ft-lb < 22,088 ft-lb → FAILS (Requires D = 5.0 ft > 4.5 ft)
• 16-inch auger (b = 1.333 ft): M_all = 17,055 × 1.333 = 22,740 ft-lb > 22,088 ft-lb → PASSES! (Requires D = 4.4 ft ≤ 4.5 ft)
• 20-inch auger (b = 1.667 ft): M_all = 28,425 ft-lb (Comfortably safe, requires D = 4.0 ft)

• Conclusion: A 16-inch diameter drilled concrete pier is the minimum standard size to satisfy the shallow 4.5 ft depth limit.
shortcut:
How Concrete Slashes Dig Depth:
1. Width Multiplier: Passive soil resistance is directly proportional to foundation width b. Increasing b from 0.625 ft (bare post) to 1.333 ft (16" concrete pier) increases passive resistance by 2.13×!
2. Depth Reduction: Because moment resistance scales with D³, doubling the diameter cuts required depth by a factor of (2)^(1/3) ≈ 1.26 (a 25% to 40% reduction in digging depth).
3. Field Application: When encountering shallow utilities, never abandon the project—specifying a 16" to 20" drilled concrete pier reduces required hole depth from over 7 ft down to 4.5 ft!
fifthGrader:
If you try to bury a skinny wooden stick only 4.5 feet in the dirt, 3,280 pounds of soil push will easily yank it right out of the ground (it needs over 7 feet of dirt to hold!).

But if you drill a wide 16-inch round hole and fill it with solid concrete around the post, the concrete acts like a giant cement boot! The dirt now has a huge 16-inch-wide cylinder pushing against it, holding the wall rock-solid at only 4.5 feet deep!

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect: A 12-inch pier only provides M_all = 17,055 ft-lb < 22,088 ft-lb. It requires D = 5.0 ft, violating the 4.5 ft site limit.

options.label: B
options.feedback: ✓ Correct! b_min = 22,088 / 17,055 = 1.295 ft (15.54 in.). The next standard auger size is 16 inches, which provides M_all = 22,740 ft-lb > 22,088 ft-lb and requires D = 4.4 ft ≤ 4.5 ft.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect: While a 24-inch pier is safe (D_req = 3.7 ft), it is not the minimum standard size. A 16-inch pier already satisfies the 4.5 ft requirement.

options.label: D
options.text: Concrete pier cannot achieve D ≤ 4.5 ft; Tiebacks required
options.feedback: Incorrect: A 16-inch or 20-inch concrete pier easily achieves D ≤ 4.5 ft without expensive tiebacks.

title: Standard Penetration Test (SPT) Data Reduction & Overburden Correction (ASTM D1586)
description:
A Standard Penetration Test (SPT) is conducted in a sand deposit at a depth of z = 20.0 ft (6.1 m) below the ground surface in accordance with ASTM D1586 and AASHTO T206. The groundwater table is measured at a depth of 8.0 ft below the ground surface.

The soil profile consists of medium-dense to dense clean sand:
• Total unit weight above GWT: γ = 120 pcf
• Saturated unit weight below GWT: γsat = 125 pcf
• Unit weight of water: γw = 62.4 pcf

The test equipment and borehole parameters are recorded as follows:
• Hammer system: Automatic trip hammer with measured energy ratio ERm = 75%
• Borehole diameter: 100 mm (4.0 in) → CB = 1.00
• Sampler: Standard split-barrel sampler without liner → CS = 1.20
• Drill rod length: 22 ft (6.7 m) → CR = 0.95
• Atmospheric reference stress: Pa = 2,000 psf (100 kPa)

During driving, the recorded blow counts for the three consecutive 6-inch (150 mm) penetration increments are:
• 0 to 6 inches: 7 blows
• 6 to 12 inches: 10 blows
• 12 to 18 inches: 14 blows

Determine the uncorrected field SPT N-value, the energy-corrected N60, the effective overburden stress σ'vo at the test depth, and the normalized SPT blow count (N1)60.

The values of uncorrected N, N60, and (N1)60 are most nearly:
hint:
1. Uncorrected Field SPT N-value (ASTM D1586):
• The blow count for the first 6 inches (0 - 6 in) is the seating drive and must be DISCARDED!
• N = N(6-12 in) + N(12-18 in) = 10 + 14 = 24 blows/ft.

2. Energy-Corrected SPT Blow Count N60:
• N60 = N × (ERm / 60) × CB × CS × CR
• Energy correction factor: CE = 75 / 60 = 1.25
• N60 = 24 × 1.25 × 1.00 × 1.20 × 0.95 = 24 × 1.425 = 34.2 blows/ft.

3. Effective Overburden Stress σ'vo at Depth z = 20 ft:
• Layer 1 (Dry sand above GWT, 0 to 8 ft): σv1 = 8 ft × 120 pcf = 960 psf
• Layer 2 (Submerged sand below GWT, 8 to 20 ft, Δz = 12 ft):
  Buoyant unit weight γ' = γsat - γw = 125 - 62.4 = 62.6 pcf
  Δσ'v = 12 ft × 62.6 pcf = 751.2 psf
• Total effective overburden: σ'vo = 960 + 751.2 = 1,711.2 psf.

4. Overburden Correction Factor CN:
• CN = (Pa / σ'vo)^0.5 = (2,000 / 1,711.2)^0.5 = (1.1688)^0.5 = 1.0811 (capped at 1.70 - 2.0).

5. Normalized Blow Count (N1)60:
• (N1)60 = N60 × CN = 34.2 × 1.0811 = 36.97 ≈ 37 blows/ft.

6. Empirical Soil Assessment:
• (N1)60 = 37 falls in the Dense Sand category (35 - 50).
• Correlated effective internal friction angle: φ' ≈ 37.5° to 38°.
shortcut:
The 3 Golden Rules of SPT Corrections on the PE Exam:
1. Never add the seating drive! N is strictly the sum of the last two 6-inch increments (N = N2 + N3). Summing all three (7 + 10 + 14 = 31) is the #1 NCEES distractor trap!
2. Always use EFFECTIVE stress σ'vo for CN, never total stress! Subtract pore water pressure below the water table (γ' = γsat - 62.4 pcf).
3. Automatic hammers deliver higher energy than standard safety hammers (75% vs 60%), which means fewer blows in the field. Correcting to N60 scales the count UP by 75/60 = 1.25!
fifthGrader:
Imagine driving a giant metal pipe into the beach with a heavy 140-pound weight that drops from 30 inches up.

The first 6 inches is just pushing the pipe into the loose stirred-up dirt at the bottom of the hole, so we throw those 7 taps in the trash!

We only count the next 12 inches: 10 blows + 14 blows = 24 blows. Then, because our automatic machine hits harder than an old rope-and-pulley, and because the sand is squeezed by 20 feet of earth, we use math formulas to translate our 24 taps into a standardized score of 37, which tells us the sand is very dense and solid!

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect: 31 occurs if you mistakenly include the 0-6 inch seating drive (7 + 10 + 14 = 31). Per ASTM D1586, the first 6 inches is seating and must always be excluded!

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect: (N1)60 = 31 occurs if you mistakenly use total overburden stress (σvo = 2,460 psf) instead of effective overburden stress (σ'vo = 1,711.2 psf). Always subtract hydrostatic pore water pressure!

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect: N60 = 28 occurs if you omit the sampler liner factor CS = 1.20 for samplers without liners.

title: Superelevation Runoff Length

fifthGrader: When a road curves, it is tilted like a banked race track — called superelevation. You cannot tilt it instantly or your car would slide. This formula tells you the minimum distance needed to gradually tilt the road.

The second curve has R2 = 400 ft and delta2 = 15 degrees. The station of the PCC (Point of Compound Curvature, where the two curves meet) is most nearly:

title: Rational Method – Peak Runoff Rate
description: The rational method must be used to determine the maximum runoff rate for a 90-acre drainage area. The time of concentration for the 50-year frequency storm is 1 hour. Intensity-Duration-Frequency (IDF) curves and a table of runoff coefficients are provided. At a 60-minute duration, the 50-year IDF curve reads i = 3.0 in/hr. The maximum runoff coefficient for a 50-year storm is C = 0.81. The maximum runoff rate is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. 160 cfs corresponds to C ≈ 0.59. Check your runoff coefficient — use the maximum C for a 50-year storm.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. 300 cfs would require C = 300 / (3.0 × 90) = 1.11, which exceeds the maximum possible value of C = 1.0.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. 340 cfs is not achievable with i = 3.0 in/hr over 90 acres. Double-check your IDF curve reading and coefficient.

hint:
Rational Method: Q = C × i × A.
Step 1: Read intensity i from the IDF curve at the storm duration (tc = 60 min) for the 50-year frequency curve.
Step 2: Look up the maximum runoff coefficient C for the land use and storm frequency.
Step 3: Multiply Q = C × i × A (area in acres, i in in/hr → Q in cfs).
shortcut:
Q = C × i × A = 0.81 × 3.0 × 90 = 218.7 ≈ 220 cfs.
Quick sanity check: if Q ÷ (i × A) > 1.0, that answer is impossible — C can never exceed 1.0.
fifthGrader: Imagine rain falling on a 90-acre field. Not all of it runs off — some soaks in. The C number tells you what fraction of rain actually becomes runoff (0 = all soaks in, 1 = all runs off). Multiply the rain rate × the fraction that runs off × the area and you get the flood flow!

title: Rational Method – Solving for Drainage Area
description: Using the rational method, a storm drain is designed for a peak flow of Q = 150 cfs. The 10-year, 30-minute storm intensity is i = 4.2 in/hr. The weighted runoff coefficient for the basin is C = 0.65. The drainage area that produces this peak flow is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Check your rearrangement: A = Q / (C × i).

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. That would require a lower intensity or coefficient.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. 90 acres would produce Q = 0.65 × 4.2 × 90 = 245 cfs, not 150 cfs.

hint: Rearrange Q = C × i × A to solve for A: A = Q / (C × i).
fifthGrader: We know how much water is coming out of the pipe (Q), how hard it's raining (i), and how much of that rain runs off (C). We're just working backwards to find the field size (A)!

A 200-acre watershed consists of three sub-areas:

• Commercial: 70 acres, C = 0.85

The composite (weighted) runoff coefficient for the entire watershed is most nearly:

fifthGrader: If half your backyard is concrete and half is grass, the average amount of rain that runs off is somewhere between a lot (concrete) and a little (grass). The bigger the piece, the more it 'pulls' the average toward itself — that's weighting!

fifthGrader: This is just the basic recipe: how much runs off (C) times how hard it rains (i) times how big the field is (A). The cool thing is the units work out perfectly — acres × in/hr = cfs!

title: Time of Concentration – Kirpich Formula
description: A watershed has a maximum flow length of L = 1,200 ft and an average slope of S = 0.015 ft/ft. Using the Kirpich formula, tc = 0.0078 × L^0.77 × S^(-0.385), the time of concentration is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Recheck your exponent arithmetic for L^0.77 and S^(-0.385).

options.label: B

options.label: D

Kirpich formula: tc = 0.0078 × L^0.77 × S^(-0.385), where tc is in minutes, L in feet, S in ft/ft.
Step 1: 1200^0.77 ≈ 210.7
Step 2: 0.015^(-0.385) ≈ 14.5
Step 3: tc = 0.0078 × 210.7 × 14.5 ≈ 23.8 min.

fifthGrader: The time of concentration is how long it takes for a raindrop falling at the farthest point in a watershed to reach the outlet. A longer path or flatter slope means it takes longer — so the storm drains slower.

If the 50-year, 30-minute storm intensity is i = 5.0 in/hr and the area A = 25 acres, the adjusted peak runoff rate is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Apply the frequency factor: C_adj = C × Cf = 0.90 × 1.25, but cap at 1.0.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. That uses the uncapped C × Cf = 1.125, which exceeds the physical maximum.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. Check that A = 25 acres and the intensity = 5.0 in/hr.

hint: The adjusted coefficient C_adj = C × Cf. If C_adj > 1.0, cap it at 1.0 (100% runoff is the physical maximum). Then Q = C_adj × i × A.
fifthGrader: A bigger storm makes more water run off, so we multiply C by a frequency factor to account for that. But you can never have MORE runoff than the rain itself — so C can never go above 1.0. It's capped!

title: SCS Curve Number – Runoff Volume
description:
A watershed has a Curve Number CN = 80 and receives a storm with total rainfall P = 4.0 inches. Using the SCS runoff equation, the direct runoff Q is most nearly:

S = (1000/CN) - 10
Q = (P - 0.2S)² / (P + 0.8S), valid when P > 0.2S

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Recalculate S = (1000/80) - 10 = 2.5 in, then apply the SCS formula.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. Double-check your denominator: P + 0.8S, not P + S.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. That would be close to Q ≈ P (very high CN). Check S with CN = 80.

fifthGrader: A Curve Number describes how 'thirsty' the soil is. CN = 100 means concrete — all rain runs off. CN = 0 would mean a giant sponge — none runs off. CN = 80 is somewhere in the middle, like compacted suburban soil.

title: SCS Curve Number – Determining CN
description:
A watershed has the following land use breakdown:
• Residential (1/4-acre lots): 500 acres, CN = 75 (Hydrologic Soil Group B)
• Paved roads with curbs: 100 acres, CN = 98
• Meadow (good condition): 200 acres, CN = 58

The composite Curve Number for the 800-acre watershed is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Compute the area-weighted average: CN = Σ(CN_i × A_i) / A_total.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. Re-check your area-weighted calculation. Make sure to use 800 acres total, not a subset.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. You may have over-weighted the paved road area.

hint: CN_composite = Σ(CN_i × A_i) / A_total. Same formula as weighted runoff coefficient — area-weighted average.
fifthGrader: Just like mixing paint colors, the final color (CN) depends on how much of each color you use. Lots of residential (75) plus a little pavement (98) plus some meadow (58) makes a medium value of about 74.

title: Return Period and Exceedance Probability
description: A storm drain is designed for the 25-year storm. The probability that this design storm will be equaled or exceeded at least once during a 10-year service life is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. 4% (= 1/25) is the annual exceedance probability — not the probability over 10 years.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect. 10% would be the annual probability for a 10-year storm, not the cumulative probability.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. Use P = 1 - (1 - 1/T)^n with T = 25, n = 10.

hint:
The probability that a T-year event is exceeded at least once in n years:
P = 1 - (1 - 1/T)^n
With T = 25 years and n = 10 years: P = 1 - (0.96)^10.
fifthGrader: A 25-year storm has a 1-in-25 (4%) chance of happening any given year. But over 10 years, those chances add up! The math shows there is about a 34% chance it happens at least once — like rolling a 4% die 10 times and hoping you never hit it.

title: Detention Basin – Storage Volume Estimate
description: A detention basin must reduce peak flow from Q_pre = 280 cfs (pre-development) to Q_post = 120 cfs (post-development allowable release). The storm hydrograph has a duration of approximately 2 hours (7,200 seconds) above the release rate. Using a simplified triangular approximation, the required storage volume is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Estimate storage as the area of the triangle between the inflow and outflow hydrographs.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. Make sure you subtract the outflow from the inflow (the net difference), not using Q_in alone.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. This result uses Q_in without subtracting Q_out, and without the 0.5 triangle factor.

hint:
For a simplified triangular hydrograph approximation:
V_storage ≈ 0.5 × (Q_in - Q_out) × t
Where t is the duration above the release rate in seconds.
fifthGrader: A detention basin is like a bathtub. Water comes in fast (the storm) but drains out slowly (the controlled release). The volume of water piling up in the tub is the area of that difference triangle — half the base times the height!

title: Manning's Equation – Downstream Pipe Sizing (Junction Box)
description:
Two identical 12-in. storm sewers flow full at a 2% slope into a junction box. A single larger pipe of the same material and slope flows out of the box. Assuming the following pipe sizes are commercially available, the minimum size of this downstream pipe (in.) designed to flow full is most nearly:

(A) 16 in.  (B) 18 in.  (C) 20 in.  (D) 24 in.

options.label: A
options.feedback: Correct! Since n and S are equal, Q ∝ D^(8/3). D_out = 12 × 2^(3/8) = 12 × 1.2968 = 15.56 in. The next commercially available size is 16 in.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect. 18 in. would work but is not the MINIMUM. The required diameter is only 15.56 in., so 16 in. is sufficient.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. 20 in. is overdesigned. The minimum required is 15.56 in. → 16 in. standard size.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. Significantly oversized. Use D_out = D_in × 2^(3/8) for pipes with the same n and S.

hint:
Key insight: When n and S are the same for all pipes, Manning's equation reduces to Q ∝ D^(8/3).
Step 1: Q_out = 2 × Q_in, so D_out^(8/3) = 2 × D_in^(8/3).
Step 2: D_out = D_in × 2^(3/8).
Step 3: D_out = 12 × 2^0.375 = 12 × 1.297 = 15.56 in.
Step 4: Round UP to next standard commercial size.
shortcut:
D_out = 12 × 2^(3/8) = 15.56 in. → round up to 16 in.
The exponent 3/8 comes from inverting the 8/3 power in Q ∝ D^(8/3).
Memorize: two identical pipes → multiply diameter by 2^(3/8) ≈ 1.297.
fifthGrader: Two garden hoses are pouring into a bucket, and one bigger hose drains it. If both small hoses are 12 inches wide, the big hose doesn't need to be 24 inches (double) — because wider pipes carry a LOT more water than their size suggests. It only needs to be about 15.6 inches, so we round up to 16 inches.

title: Manning's Equation – Pipe Flow Rate (Full Flow)
description: A 24-inch diameter concrete storm sewer (n = 0.013) flows full on a slope of S = 0.005. The discharge Q using Manning's equation is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Check your unit conversions: D = 24 in = 2 ft, A = π(2)²/4 = 3.14 ft², R = D/4 = 0.5 ft.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. Check slope term: S^(1/2) = (0.005)^0.5 = 0.0707, not 0.005.

shortcut:
Q = (1.486/0.013) × π × (2²/4) × (0.5)^0.667 × √0.005
= 114.3 × 3.1416 × 0.6300 × 0.07071 = 16.0 cfs.
Note: Some reference tables give slightly different Q depending on rounding — always show your work.
fifthGrader: Manning's equation is the recipe for how fast water flows through a pipe. A wider pipe (bigger A), smoother walls (smaller n), and steeper slope (bigger S) all make water flow faster. R is the 'effective width' — for a full circle it's just D/4.

title: Manning's Equation – Required Pipe Slope
description: A 18-inch diameter corrugated metal pipe (n = 0.024) must carry Q = 6.5 cfs when flowing full. The minimum slope required is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Rearrange Manning's for S: S = [Q × n / (1.486 × A × R^(2/3))]²

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. Check R^(2/3) for D = 1.5 ft: R = 0.375 ft, R^(2/3) = 0.525.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. That slope is too steep. Re-check your area and hydraulic radius calculations.

fifthGrader: If you need a specific amount of water to flow through a pipe, and you know the pipe size and roughness, you work backwards to find how steep the pipe needs to slope. Steeper = faster flow!

title: Manning's Equation – Hydraulic Radius of Partially Full Pipe
description: A 36-inch circular pipe flows at a depth of d = 18 inches (half-full). The hydraulic radius R for this flow condition is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. For a semicircle, A = πD²/8 and P = πD/2. Use R = A/P.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct! At half-full: A = πD²/8 = π(3)²/8 = 3.534 ft². Wetted perimeter P = πD/2 = π(3)/2 = 4.712 ft. R = A/P = 3.534/4.712 = 0.75 ft. Note: for a half-full circle, R = D/4.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. At half-full, R = D/4 exactly for a circular pipe — not larger.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. That would be R = D/4 for D = 4.5 ft. Use D = 3 ft (36 inches).

hint:
For a circular pipe flowing half-full:
• Flow area A = πD²/8 (half the full-circle area)
• Wetted perimeter P = πD/2 (half the circumference)
• R = A/P = (πD²/8) / (πD/2) = D/4
• R = 36 in / 4 = 9 in = 0.75 ft
shortcut: Key fact: A circular pipe flowing half-full has the SAME hydraulic radius as when it flows full (R = D/4). R = D/4 = 3.0/4 = 0.75 ft. This is a great fact to memorize for the PE exam!
fifthGrader: The hydraulic radius tells us how efficiently the pipe cross-section carries water. Surprisingly, a pipe that's exactly half full has the same hydraulic radius as when it's completely full — because when you halve both the area and the wetted perimeter, R = D/4 in both cases!

title: Manning's Equation – Velocity in Open Channel
description: A trapezoidal irrigation channel has a bottom width b = 6 ft, side slopes of 2H:1V, a flow depth y = 3 ft, Manning's n = 0.025, and a channel slope S = 0.0008. The flow velocity using Manning's equation is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Calculate the trapezoidal A and P first: A = (b + zy)y, P = b + 2y√(1+z²).

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. Recheck your wetted perimeter: P = b + 2y√(1 + z²) with z = 2 (2H:1V).

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. You may have used R = y instead of the true hydraulic radius R = A/P.

fifthGrader: Imagine a V-shaped irrigation ditch. The velocity depends on how wide and deep it is, how rough its walls are (n), and how steeply it slopes. A smooth, wide, steep channel carries water much faster than a rough, narrow, flat one.

title: Manning's – Three Identical Pipes Merging
description: Three identical 15-inch storm sewers, all with the same Manning's n and slope S, flow full and discharge into a single junction box. A single downstream pipe with the same n and S must carry all three flows when flowing full. The minimum diameter of the downstream pipe is most nearly:

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect. The required diameter is 22.2 in., which exceeds 21 in. Round UP to the next standard size.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Correct! D_out = 15 × 3^(3/8) = 15 × 1.482 = 22.2 in. The next standard pipe size is 24 in.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. 30 in. is oversized. The required minimum diameter is 22.2 in.

hint:
Same approach as two-pipe merger, but scale factor is 3 instead of 2:
Q_out = 3 × Q_in → D_out^(8/3) = 3 × D_in^(8/3)
D_out = D_in × 3^(3/8)
D_out = 15 × 3^0.375 = 15 × 1.482 = 22.2 in. → round UP to 24 in.
shortcut:
For N identical pipes merging: D_out = D_in × N^(3/8)
N=2: multiply by 2^(3/8) = 1.297
N=3: multiply by 3^(3/8) = 1.482
N=4: multiply by 4^(3/8) = 1.682
fifthGrader: Three garden hoses into one bigger hose — the big hose grows, but not three times bigger! Because pipes are circles, volume scales with diameter to the 8/3 power. So three 15-inch pipes only need a 22.2-inch pipe — we round up to 24 inches for a real pipe.

title: Manning's – Velocity in Circular Pipe (Partial Flow)
description: A 24-inch concrete pipe (n = 0.013) on a slope S = 0.004 flows at a depth of 12 inches (half-full). The average flow velocity is most nearly:

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Recall that at half-full, R = D/4, same as full flow. Compute V = (1.486/n) × R^(2/3) × S^(1/2).

options.label: B
options.feedback: Correct! At half-full, R = D/4 = 0.5 ft. V = (1.486/0.013) × (0.5)^(2/3) × (0.004)^(1/2) = 114.3 × 0.630 × 0.0632 = 4.55 ft/s ≈ use full-flow proportionality → V_half ≈ V_full.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. Velocity at half-full equals velocity at full flow (R is the same). It does NOT exceed full-flow velocity.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. That would require a much steeper slope or smoother pipe material.

hint:
Key fact: For a circular pipe, the velocity at HALF-FULL equals the velocity at FULL flow,
because R = D/4 in both cases (A/P simplifies identically).
V = (1.486/n) × (D/4)^(2/3) × S^(1/2)
With D = 2.0 ft, n = 0.013, S = 0.004.
fifthGrader: Counterintuitive fact: a pipe flowing exactly half-full sends water at the SAME speed as when full! The water has half the cross-section area, but also half the pipe wall dragging against it — so they cancel out.

title: Manning's – Normal Depth in Rectangular Channel
description: A rectangular concrete channel (n = 0.013) has a bottom width b = 8 ft and a longitudinal slope S = 0.001. The design discharge is Q = 200 cfs. The normal depth y_n is most nearly:

options.label: C
options.feedback: Incorrect. At y = 5.0 ft the channel would carry more than 200 cfs. Normal depth is less than 5 ft.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. Too deep — this channel would carry well over 300 cfs at y = 6.2 ft.

hint:
Trial-and-error or iterative solution:
• Guess y, compute A = by, P = b + 2y, R = A/P
• Compute Q = (1.486/n) × A × R^(2/3) × S^(1/2)
• If Q_calc < Q_design, increase y; if Q_calc > Q_design, decrease y.
Target: Q = 200 cfs with b = 8 ft, n = 0.013, S = 0.001.
shortcut:
Try y = 3.8 ft: A = 30.4, P = 15.6, R = 1.949, R^(2/3) = 1.584
Q = (1.486/0.013) × 30.4 × 1.584 × 0.03162 = 114.3 × 30.4 × 1.584 × 0.03162 ≈ 174 cfs.
On the PE exam, answer choices are spread enough to identify the right bracket quickly.
fifthGrader: Normal depth is the depth a channel naturally flows at for a given flow rate and slope — like cruise control for water. You find it by guessing, checking if the math gives the right flow, and adjusting up or down.

title: Manning's – Full vs. Partial Flow Proportionality
description:
A 30-inch concrete pipe (n = 0.013, S = 0.003) flows full at Q_full. At what depth d (in inches) does the flow rate equal exactly 0.80 × Q_full?

Use the standard hydraulic elements chart relationship: at d/D ≈ 0.82, Q/Q_full ≈ 0.80.

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. d/D = 0.5 corresponds to Q/Q_full ≈ 0.50, not 0.80.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect. d/D = 0.70 corresponds to Q/Q_full ≈ 0.70.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Correct! From hydraulic elements chart, Q/Q_full = 0.80 occurs at d/D ≈ 0.82. d = 0.82 × 30 = 24.6 in.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. d = 30 in. is the full-pipe condition (Q/Q_full = 1.0).

hint:
Use the dimensionless hydraulic elements chart for circular pipes:
• d/D = 0.50 → Q/Q_full ≈ 0.50
• d/D = 0.70 → Q/Q_full ≈ 0.70
• d/D = 0.82 → Q/Q_full ≈ 0.80
• d/D = 0.94 → Q/Q_full ≈ 1.00 (maximum flow occurs above half-full!)
Find d/D for Q/Q_full = 0.80 from the chart, then d = (d/D) × D.
shortcut: d = 0.82 × 30 = 24.6 in. from hydraulic elements chart at Q/Q_full = 0.80.
fifthGrader: Here's a surprising fact: a circular pipe actually carries its MAXIMUM flow at about 94% full — not completely full! That's because at 94% full, the 'wetted perimeter' (pipe wall creating friction) hasn't grown as fast as the flow area. The hydraulic elements chart captures all these relationships.

title: Manning's – Minimum Velocity for Self-Cleansing
description: A sanitary sewer is designed with n = 0.013 and slope S = 0.0030. The pipe diameter is 10 inches. The average velocity in the pipe when flowing full is most nearly (check if it meets the minimum self-cleansing velocity of 2.0 ft/s for sanitary sewers):

options.label: A
options.feedback: Incorrect. Recalculate: D = 10/12 = 0.833 ft, R = D/4 = 0.2083 ft, R^(2/3) = 0.347.

options.label: B
options.feedback: Incorrect. 2.5 ft/s would meet the 2.0 ft/s minimum. Re-read the question.

options.label: C
options.feedback: Correct! V = (1.486/0.013) × (0.2083)^(2/3) × (0.003)^(1/2) = 114.3 × 0.347 × 0.05477 = 2.17 ft/s. This exceeds 2.0 ft/s. Closest listed answer showing it meets the minimum.

options.label: D
options.feedback: Incorrect. That velocity is too high for these pipe parameters.

hint:
Manning's velocity: V = (1.486/n) × R^(2/3) × S^(1/2)
• D = 10 in = 0.833 ft
• R = D/4 = 0.2083 ft
• R^(2/3) = (0.2083)^0.667 = 0.347
• V = (1.486/0.013) × 0.347 × √(0.003)
Compare result to 2.0 ft/s minimum self-cleansing velocity.
fifthGrader: Sewer pipes need water to flow fast enough to push solids along — otherwise they clog! Engineers call 2.0 ft/s the 'self-cleansing velocity'. If the pipe flows too slowly, gunk builds up and you have a very smelly problem.
